subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, October 30, consideration of the motion of Mr. Hockin that Bill C-14, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-14 before us today is a Bill which came out of the February, 1986, Budget. It is a rather slim Bill; it does not have very many pages. However, the contents of it add up to a very heavy burden for the average taxpayer. The Bill legislates approval for a number of tax increases with which Canadians have been coping for some months now.
We must remember that the tax increases in the last Budget were on top of the tax increases in the first Budget of the Conservative Government in May, 1985. As I said, it adds up to a heavy burden for the average taxpayer.
For example, the federal manufacturers sales tax has been raised three times in 18 months. The tax rate is now 3 per cent higher and, as well, the tax base was considerably broadened to cover more items. As a result Canadians are paying about $3.5 billion more per year.
The Government says that it needs this tax revenue to fight the deficit. We all care that the deficit should be reduced, but surely the Government must also be sensitive to how the deficit will be reduced.
I do not think enough attention has been paid to the role which unemployment has played in the deficit we are now facing. During recession years when we were averaging between $11 billion and $12 billion per year in unemployment insurance, it was certainly a major factor in our deficit. Also, unemployed people do not pay income tax. They do not make purchases on which they would pay sales tax. Surely if we are seriously attempting to tackle the deficit, especially now in the fourth year of recovery, we should be addressing ourselves much more to the question of unemployment.
These sales taxes run quite a risk of slowing down economic recovery and of adding to unemployment. In order for our employment record to stand still we need economic growth of 3 per cent a year. We are not getting that at this time. In their budget speeches government Members spoke about economic recovery. However, more independent observers have pointed out that we have problems which, I believe, are in no small way due to the Government's policy of "tax, tax, tax".
[DOT] (mo)
The Government's first economic statement was presented in November, 1984, very shortly after it came into power. In that statement the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) set out his basic principles for economic recovery. He said: "Deficit reduction is the key to rebuilding confidence and confidence is the key to growth and job creation". Quite a lot of time has passed since November, 1984, and it is interesting to hear what economic analysts are saying. In the October issue of the Business Conditions Bulletin published by Woods Gordon one reads:
It is becoming increasingly apparent that economic progress in 1986 has been very limited. Overall, the economy has been at a virtual standstill since the beginning of the year.
Data Resources of Canada says:
The choppy and only tepid path of real economic growth has had a predictable impact on the labour market: employment growth has stagnated since late last year.
I have no wish to attack the Government again about broken promises or to be unduly negative. However, no one will easily forget the constant refrain of "jobs, jobs, jobs" in the 1984 election campaign. Therefore the Government must expect to be held accountable for policies which work against an increase in employment.
We have seen increasing attempts by this Government to tax its way out of the deficit by way of sale taxes rather than income taxes. Sales taxes have, for very good reason, been traditionally regarded as regressive. While income tax is related to one's ability to pay, sales tax is charged on every

November 3, 1986
Excise Tax Act
product regardless of ability to pay. It hits the poor harder because they have less discretionary income and are obliged to spend more of their income for the necessities of life. Even so, the Government's recent announcement of its guidelines for tax reform included a mention that the Government intends to rely more on sales tax revenue in the future.
There is some evidence that all these sales taxes are having a dampening effect on consumer confidence and that consumer spending is down, with the resultant effect on the labour market. The Minister of Finance recently announced that all the tax increases which consumers have been asked to shoulder have not worked and that the deficit will be higher than forecast.
Let us consider some of the specifics of Bill C-14 in this context. The numbers in this Bill and those given in the February 26 Budget Papers add up to very large tax increases. Between now and 1990 Canadians will have to pay an additional $6 billion. In 1986 alone there will be an additional burden of S820 million. The 1 per cent increase in the sales tax will cost Canadian taxpayers $700 million. The increase in tax on alcohol will probably amount to another $125 million. In 1987 Canadians will pay an additional $1.2 billion in taxes. They will pay an additional $1,355 billion in 1988 and $1,455 billion in 1990, for a total of $6.1 billion.
Measures previously announced and adopted resulted in a 2 per cent increase in sales tax. That, combined with a 1 per cent increase in Bill C-14, amounts to a 3 per cent increase. This is a very heavy burden which seriously affects jobs and poor families. We are now in the fourth year of recovery and the Government's taxing policies have slowed down economic growth. There is great risk that this will continue with very serious effects on our already too high unemployment rate.
I have an article dated October 31 headed "Is Michael Wilson a Reverse Robin Flood?" The article makes the point that this continued emphasis on sales tax will hit the poor hardest and that the likely beneficiaries will be the rich. If the future policy is to put more and more emphasis on sales tax rather than on income tax this will be compounded because the poor, who now pay little or no income tax, will not benefit from the proposed reduction in personal income tax but will pay greatly for the business transfer tax which is essentially a sales tax.
The Minister has spoken of increasing corporation taxes, which I understand the New Democratic Party is in favour of. One must remember that in the long run it is people who pay corporation taxes. If corporate taxes are increased, those taxes will be passed on to the consumer who will end up paying for them.
The Government claims to be sensitive to the relationship of social and economic goals. Yet there is disturbingly little in the Speech from the Throne about an economic strategy for Canada, and this kind of Bill does not inspire confidence. With
over one million Canadians still out of work, unemployment is a very real problem that has proven resistant to the Government's efforts to date. Clearly the Government will be more successful in meeting social policy objectives if it has the means at its disposal. The means will not be there if the economy is not performing well.
This Bill runs a very serious risk of damaging the economy. The Government has talked a great deal about enhancing investor confidence and indeed, if there is investor confidence, businesses can start up, businesses can expand and thereby create jobs so that the unemployed can go back to work and young people can again begin believing in the future.
Flowever, will we get increased confidence from a Bill that piles on tax after tax, reduces consumer spending, and leaves people with less to save?
There is no more urgent problem facing the country at this time than unemployment. It is a problem for individuals, families, and for our whole economy. It has been said that work may not be a blessing, but the absence of it certainly is a curse. Unemployment is a demoralizing and soul-destroying experience. It shatters ideals and ambitions and puts a blight on family life. It lies at the root of any number of social ills. On the other hand, an employed person is paying taxes, spending money on consumer goods and probably saving, since Canadians are great savers. He or she is contributing to government revenues which are the means for providing all social programs for all Canadians.
It is very disturbing to see that the Government is not putting more effort into creating the climate that will assure Canadians of the jobs, jobs, jobs, they have been promised. Instead, all we are seeing are taxes, taxes, taxes.

Member comment particularly on what this $15,000 cut-off point means in terms of a definition of poverty, or low income?

Mr. Speaker, I would like the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) to expand on her comments with respect to corporation taxes. In the seven years that I have been here, I have been amazed at how essentially dishonest Parliament has become with the population. There seems to be a feeling that taxes, or revenues, will come from someone else.
1 know that the members of the New Democratic Party particularly argue for dramatic increases in corporation tax. I agree with my friend opposite that it just means they will increase the price of their products to ordinary Canadians and it simply masks the fact that it is people who pay taxes rather than some mythical third party.
Is it the official position of the Liberal Party that corporation tax should be kept down for that reason? If not, what percentage of tax does she believe the corporations should pay?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is a very loaded question but let me attempt to answer it. First, I can understand very well the outrage that we hear from people such as those in my constituency who work extremely hard to buy homes and support children on salaries that are well under $30,000 a year. People like that may hear of corporations being able to write off the costs of their corporate jets and so on. They often feel a certain outrage that they are carrying a very high burden. I think we have to respond to that outrage and be very sure we have the clear facts.
Excise Tax Act
The Auditor General, I think, has done quite a good job in pointing out the results of taxes forgone, or the so-called tax expenditures. Indeed, a former member of the Conservative Party, when he chaired the Public Accounts Committee, made a very useful contribution to the debate on tax expenditures. So I believe we have to be sensitive and understand people's outrage and their need for explanations.
That being said, we also have to be very sure that we are dealing with practicalities rather than with ideology. Some phrases like "corporate welfare bums" are great in a campaign, but when one looks at the facts it really comes down to the point that, if a corporation is paying more taxes, in most cases that gets passed on one way or another to the consumer. The real answer is not that corporations should pay less and individuals should pay more. The real answer is for us all to know the facts and to have a very clear handle on what tax expenditures are coming in. Over the years, indeed, our taxation law has grown more and more complex. Tax expenditures have increased in complexity. I think our first responsibility, our first task, is to simplify matters so we all know what we are dealing with. Then we must be very clear about what the burden is and on whom.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think we have a certain amount of fuzzy thinking on the part of the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) and on the part of the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) who asked the question regarding the passing on of corporation taxes to the consumer. I think the Hon. Member for Trinity expressed it very well. The labourer, the person who goes out and by the sweat of his brow makes his living and pays taxes not only through income tax, but in excise taxes which are being increased by this particular measure, has to be separated to some extent from the person who takes the profits of the corporation for which he has done nothing specifically. He has used his investment capital in some way to receive these profits and it is the profits which are being taxed in corporations, or what are not being taxed in corporations. There are large numbers of corporations which are not being taxed at all. That tax break, theoretically, will be passed on by dividends to the shareholders, not to the consumers. So what we are doing is reducing the amount of return from investment. That is what is intended here. Does the Hon. Member not recognize that reducing the profits of corporations is a more equitable way of taxation than the present consumer tax or income tax directly on an individual?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with respect to Bill C-14. I followed with great interest the debate of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Trinty (Miss Nicholson), who was not able to outline the position of the Liberal Party since it is in the process of being developed. That probably explains why the Liberal Party is doing so well in the polls.
When a Party is in opposition it is wise to be on the side of every issue. Members of the Liberal Party have tried very carefully to walk that line, but as we come closer to the general election the Liberal Party will have to declare its position on some of these major policy issues. The minute the Party does that, 10 per cent or 15 per cent of the population will say that they do not like the position at all and that the Liberal Party is no better than the New Democratic Party or the Conservative Party. Members of the Liberal Party will find that their standing at the polls will be hurt as they come to take decisions, and that the Government will then look a lot better.
We must appreciate where we are as a nation and where we were when the Conservative Party came to power. At that time the Liberals had been the governing authority for 20 years. They stayed in power during the period 1972 to 1974 with the direct and open support of the New Democratic Party. During that time they put in place a series of economic and fiscal policies which led the country into a national debt situation which, per capita, is almost three or four times greater than that of our immediate neighbour to the south, the United States of America.
It is in the context of the largest per capita debt that we have to consider the sales tax and excise tax increases. We have to consider the reductions, and they will be dramatic ones, in corporate exemptions and in the tax expenditure account, as well as an increase in income taxes, particularly on the rich as a result of the minimum tax. When we assumed power we decided as an over-all policy that there would have to be increases in corporate taxes and in income taxes, especially those on the rich, and also increases in income taxes on upper-income earners, not necessarily the very rich. At the same time we recognized that there would have to be dramatic cuts in government expenditures.
We are now moving on all fronts, even in terms of indexing. What the Liberals and members of the NDP did was index the expenditure side of the federal Government and deductions against revenue sources to Government. So when we went through the period of high inflation we saw that the expenditures increased proportionately, just as the revenues dropped proportionately. This was so because both sides of the equation had been indexed, which is why we now have a national debt of well over $200 billion at the federal level alone.
I often hear people say that federal debt is not significant because we owe it to ourselves. The argument has some validity with respect to federal debt. But what is not told to our citizens is that, because we at the federal level absorb all the
November 3, 1986

domestic savings, primarily through Treasury Bills, Canada Savings Bonds and those types of instruments, we have left the provinces, all Crown corporations, federal and provincial, and private corporations exposed. Private corporations are exposed in that they now have to go offshore in search of funds. The provinces, Crown corporations and private corporations owe over $90 billion outside Canada. This debt poses a great threat to our senior citizens and our lower-income earners.
If international interest rates rise, as they may well rise, that means more dollars have to flow out of the country to service the over $90 billion foreign debt. That move will drive interest rates higher, and it could cause our dollar to drop. This in turn will have a massive impact on our senior citizens. As a country we are faced with the dilemma of having a huge national debt. While our per capita debt is much higher than that of the U.S., we are higher even than Mexico, Brazil, and Third World countries, which is causing concern to our international banking system.
We are also faced with the fact that at March 31 next year we will have finished another fiscal year. Canadians need to appreciate this fact. Even with all of the changes which we have implemented we will have to add another $32 billion to the national debt, which will bring it up to $250 billion as opposed to $220 billion. To service this extra debt of $32 billion next year's Budget will have to be increased by $3 billion just to cover the interest on the increase. Some 93 per cent of today's deficit is the result of paying interest on money borrowed to finance yesterday's deficit. That is the dilemma which we are in now.
I can remember that as recently as 1968 we did not have a deficit in this country. We had a small national debt even after having developed our huge nation, bought the West, opened it up, and fought two world wars. For the first 100 years of Confederation the national debt amounted to $18 billion and the nation's budget had no deficit at all. In fact there were surpluses. After the Conservatives came to power following 18 years of a Liberal-NDP coalition, the national debt had risen to over $200 billion and our national yearly deficit was over $30 billion.

speechtext: It's your debt now; you're maintaining it.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
It is true that it is now our debt. We have had to take hard decisions to counter it. We want Canadians to understand that we are in a dilemma that was not of their making. It was a position gotten into as a result of conscious and deliberate political decisions taken by the Liberal Party. The NDP cannot get around the fact that it aided and abetted the Liberals, particularly during the 1972 to 1974 period.
My friend opposite spoke about unemployment. There is no doubt that it is serious. I think we must also appreciate that the deficit is so large that even if we took one million unemployed and gave them jobs paying $30,000 a year, if the economy were such that we could do that, a person making $30,000 per year would pay about $6,000 in federal income taxes. So one million people at $6,000 would give us an extra
Excise Tax Act
revenue of $6 billion. However, the deficit would still be $32 billion; and if we deducted $6 billion from that we would still have a deficit of $26 billion. Of course the unemployment account would go down by perhaps another $6 billion. However, we would still have a deficit of around $20 billion. This sets out the magnitude of the cursed deficit which we face. We spend about $25 billion to service this debt. If we did not have the debt then we would have a balanced budget today. The country would be strong and we would be able to get into making deficits to create jobs for our young people. However, when one starts with a huge deficit it makes it very difficult.
I also wish to clarify another point because I think too many Members try to pass it off as if there is someone in our society who makes a huge amount of money and there is someone else who can pay.
We need to start with the following facts. If one earns $30,000 a year that person is already at the 85.54 percentile point. This means that if one earns $30,000 from all sources there are only 14.46 per cent of people who pay more in taxes than that person.

Mr. Speaker, I tell my hon. friend that the figures I have quoted were taken out of income tax statistics this morning. They show that if one has an income of $30,000 per annum one is already at the 85 percentile point. If a person makes $50,000 per year, less than what we as Members of Parliament make, he is at the 98.1 percentile level. Less than 2 per cent of the people in our society make more than $50,000 per year. In fact that is not 2 per cent of the people in our society but 2 per cent of the people who pay income tax and file income tax returns. That indicates to me that there is no other large group in society that could pay. If we took every cent from people who made over $100,000, that would barely touch the deficit.
We should be honest with our fellow citizens. We should say: "Look gang, there is no one out there except you and me and ultimately the deficit has to be picked up by you and me". As Members of Parliament who make $55,000 per year, we are probably at the 99th percentile point. We should be thinking of what extras we can pay.
On an entirely personal note, it seems to me to be wrong for members of the New Democratic Party to argue for the

continuance of universality with respect to family allowances-they want to continue to receive it themselves-while people are standing in food lines. Somehow, that strikes me as being wrong. I think we as Members of Parliament should face that and should realize that we have to pay more. In a sense, we will be paying more because of the minimum tax.
I was glad to hear the comments of the Hon. Member for Trinity vis-a-vis the corporate tax. I have argued here that corporate tax is very much like a sales tax. It is passed right through to the citizens. It is the citizen who is buying shoes and clothes who pays the corporate tax.
If I had my druthers, I would have the following tax system: every time we as elected Members of Parliament went to our constituents to tell them of a beautiful program that we wanted to give to them, we should have to say in the same breath: "Here is where the money will come from and this is how much you are going to have to pay, Mr. Farmer, and this is how much you are going to have to pay, Mr. Shoemaker". If we did that, we would hear the people saying: "We do not need that program. Thank you very much, Mr. Member of Parliament. It might be a great idea, but we would rather keep the money in our pockets and decide how to spend it".
I have often argued in the House that I would rather leave the money with the people and let them decide how to spend it. I fundamentally believe that millions and millions of individual decisions taken by citizens in their communities and homes for their own best interests would lead to a spending policy that is wiser than the Liberal-NDP policy which has been to tax the money into Ottawa so that the politicans and the Cabinet may decide who will win and who will lose.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: You're the one who's taxing it with this Bill.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Yes, we have to say to the people that, as a result of the policies the Liberals and NDPs put in, the people will have to pay. For so many years we had all of these wonderful policies. We all liked the programs, but we paid low taxes. There was a cash flow difference which gave us the appearance of wealth. As a result of having good programs and low taxes, we paid too much for land and for our businesses. It has to come to an end because the trick is that we were borrowing the money and the deficit started to rise.
In 1968 only about 5 per cent of tax revenues went to pay interest on the debt. That figure went to 10 per cent, then to 15 per cent, and then to 20 per cent. We in opposition were saying that it was not right to pay a higher and higher percentage of our revenue, right off the top, to service the debt. Suddenly over 33 per cent of the revenue started going right off the top to pay interest on the debt. That money is not available to be used to create new programs. The people who are rich and have so much money that they can lend some to the Government with no risk, sit back and lend that money to the Government while the Government pays 33 per cent of all its revenues to maintain that loan. This means that we are losing the middle class. The rich are becoming fabulously rich while those in the middle class lose the benefits of government
programs. We have to face up to that. We have to make a very difficult adjustment and I think the people are beginning to see that we must do so.
There is no doubt that there has been an increase in the direct taxes payable by the people. I do not think members of the NDP or the Liberal Party will be able to argue against that because of the European experience. Several European countries are run by socialist Governments. These Governments have moved almost unanimously to value-added taxes, an indirect tax. This is another way in which Governments are dishonest with their people. They take the money from them indirectly rather than directly through an income tax.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: And you're going to do the same thing.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: That's what you're doing.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: Yes, exactly. That is what is happening in Canada. People need to understand that.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: Are you saying that you are being dishonest today?

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
My friend from Winnipeg always gets very exercised when people try to tell the citizens what truly is happening. Socialist Governments in Europe use a value-added tax of about 12 per cent to 15 per cent. If we in Canada switched to a business transfer tax or a value-added tax, it would only have to be in the 2.5 per cent to 3 per cent range to raise the same amount of money as we raise through our tax system.
That the value-added tax in Europe is about 15 per cent tells us how much money those socialist Governments take from their people in order to redistribute it in the way the politicians want. They do this rather than leaving the money with the citizens and letting them decide how they want to spend their own money. Canadians should look forward to that if they want the Government to continue taking money away from them and deciding who will be the winner. Decisions about who will be the winner are never based on economic factors. They are based on being friends of the Government or on being in an industry that the politicians, for the time being, feel is a good industry. However, that is never the same as what the market-place would decide.
Canadians need to appreciate the fact that taxes will go up, up, and up. It does not matter which Party governs the country. However, Canadians are better off with us because we are trying to get them to appreciate the role of government and how obtrusive it has become. I hope Canadians will react by saying that they want less government control and that they want the money left with them so that they may decide how to spend it themselves.

If my friend opposite is saying that the high interest rates that we have endured as a nation were the result of the amendments to the Bank Act, I will simply disagree with him on that point. Those changes to the Bank Act which permitted foreign banks to come in and compete with the five banks that had a monopoly position in this country for decades was not the decision that increased the interest rates. The reason that the interest rates went up to 18, 19, and 21 per cent, was as a result of accumulated deficits. Countries all over the world have lived through this before. We seem to be not capable of learning from it. Any time there is a Government, whether it is a king chipping or clipping the coins, or turning on the printing presses, which is what happened here, that leads to deficits that in time automatically leads to an interest rate increase, inflation, higher interest rates, and then the collapse.
What we are enduring right now is the collapse at the end of this 15 year period of madness. That collapse is very difficult. We have whole towns going out of business. We have farmers by the tens of thousands having to give up on farming. Every year there are tens of thousands of small businesses that go out of business. We are now into the adjustment phase. There is no doubt that when we get through it the people who survive are going to be well positioned and the country is going to continue on. However, it would not have been necessary to go through all of that if parliamentarians had stood up, as members of our Party did for years, and argued against those deficits. It is a fundamental deceit when governments say to people that we will give you this wonderful program and you can keep your low tax. It is true that in the short run you can, but ultimately people have to pay.
It is people who pay the taxes and create the wealth. If you do not give people a chance to get a job, which is what happens after inflation and the adjustment phase, they cannot create the wealth. I say sincerely that I think that all of those programs, offered without having a corresponding tax, has
hurt the poor more than if the scenario of the late sixties had been carried on where the Government, if it had a program, had increased the taxes so there were no deficits.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate. Bill C-14, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act is a very crucial debate. This Bill comes out of the previous Budget. It is important for Canadians to understand the essential message of the Bill before the House. In a nutshell it indicates that the Conservative approach to taxation is unfair. The Conservative Government is increasing the tax burden of ordinary Canadian families in an inequitable fashion.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is very important to everyone, that all Canadians understand the message the Conservative Government is sending them with this legislation. The Government's approach to the tax system is unfair. It is proposing to increase the tax burden for the average family, and they way it has chosen to do this is unfair.
I should like to take a look at the history of our taxation system. First I will make a few comments about the last 20 years and the direction of that system. Also, I will look closer at what the Conservative Government is doing today and has been doing for the last couple of years. Then I will make some comments about the future and about what is likely to happen in the taxation area.
Two important trends have stood out in the taxation system over the last 20 years. These trends are important to ordinary Canadians in that they affect the burden of taxation, where it falls, and the extent of it. The first trend which has been evident for the last 20 years concerns the responsibility of paying for the expense of Government, whether the money is used wisely or wasted, as was the case in the transfer of a prison to the riding of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). It was a clear waste of some $41 million according to the Auditor General's report. The burden of taxation has been placed more and more upon the shoulders of ordinary people, and profitable corporations have been carrying less and less of the responsibility of paying for government services. While corporations exist to make a profit, they are also citizens in a sense. Most corporations have a public relations arm or team to ensure that their image is a good one, that they are seen as good corporate citizens. It is incumbent upon them to carry their fair share of the burden.
However, over the last 20 years, under both Conservative and Liberal Governments, the burden of taxation has fallen more heavily upon the backs of individual Canadians, while

November 3, 1986
corporations have tended to walk away with a lighter and lighter load.
It is not surprising in that context to have heard the comments of the Hon. Member in the Liberal Party who questioned New Democrats raising the matter about the share of the taxation burden carried by corporations. She claimed that if the taxes on corporations were increased, they would just pass them on to consumers and, therefore, there was no use in taxing them. That analysis ignores the fact that profitable corporations can absorb a portion of the taxation burden. Corporations should not always be free to raise their prices whenever they want. Market forces can force corporations to absorb some of the costs rather than the burden always being passed on to consumers.
Another major trend in taxation has been that the income tax system has become less and less progressive. A generally accepted notion of the income tax system is that it is a way in which people can pay their fair share. Those who earn more pay more because they are capable of paying more; those who earn less pay less because it is more difficult for them to pay taxes. This principle has been eroding in a very significant way over the last 20 years. I wanted to make those two fundamental points about the taxation system over the last couple of decades under both Liberal and Conservative Governments.
Another point needs to be mentioned. The Auditor General indicated in his report that the taxation system was very complicated, that the system of giving tax write-offs to corporations was very complicated, and that it was very difficult to trace just exactly where public money was going. Every time someone is forgiven taxes, in effect it is an expenditure of public money. Obviously when the Government starts a program, it is an expenditure of public money. However, when it fails to collect taxes, it is also an expenditure of public money. The whole system of write-offs riddling the taxation system and giving breaks to corporations for various reasons has become so complicated that it is difficult, if not impossible, to trace the impact of any particular write-off. The use of the taxation system as an economic instrument is being undermined, and the capacity of using the taxation system to steer the economy is being weakened. Since the system cannot be understood, it is not only unmanageable but is less equitable.

Mr. Speaker, during the last 20 years, there have been two important developments in our tax system. First, the tax burden for corporations and individuals has changed, in that the burden has been shifted to the average Canadian and away from the corporations.
Second, Mr. Speaker, personal income tax has traditionally been progressive, in that those who earned more, paid more and people who earned less, paid less. However, this concept is weakening and today, personal income tax has become less progressive than it was before.
Excise Tax Act

I should like to comment about what is going on today with Bill C-14, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act, and what has been going on for the last couple of years under the present Conservative Government.
It is important to note that since that Government has been in office it has managed to increase taxes on an ordinary Canadian family by $1,305. That is an enormous increase for an ordinary family, by which I mean one with two dependent children, earning $35,000 a year. Of that $1,305 Conservative tax increase, some $845 is in sales and excise taxes. That is the significance of this legislation.
Why do I raise questions about the increase in sales and excise taxes? Not only because people are strapped for money and this is not the time to be increasing taxes, but also because the way these taxes are being increased is unfair. Sales taxes are hidden taxes. They are not, as my friend across the way suggested earlier, an honest representation of government policy direction. They are a way of raising taxes without people really noticing. Louis XIV of France, a master at raising taxes, had a finance Minister who helped him raise the money for the grand palaces which he built and lived in. That Minister described taxation as a matter of being able to pluck as many feathers from the goose as possible with the least amount of hissing. That describes what the Conservative Government is doing today in relying so heavily upon sales and excise taxes.
Five minutes, is it? Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I appreciate your letting me know how much time I have left in my speech because time passes faster than I realize.

To conclude, Bill C-14 sends a clear message to Canadians that the Conservative approach to taxation is unfair. It increases the burden on ordinary Canadian families. Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in the debate on Bill C-14, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act. It is important to make it clear for the people who are listening to this debate that a majority of the measures that we are discussing in this legislation came into effect with the introduction of the Budget in 1986. They are not new or additional increases, we are simply going through the process of passing legislation to legalize those measures.
This Bill is an integral part of our over-all approach to economic renewal. We must keep reinforcing what we said in September, 1984, about our goals and our objectives as a Government. One of our major priorities was economic renewal.
Unfortunately, we must keep harking back to what the circumstances were at that time. After so many years of Liberal rule we were in a terrible deficit situation. Spending had risen by an average of 23 per cent per year, the gross national debt had grown by 50 per cent, and debt service costs had grown by 85 per cent. In fact, from 1981-82 to 1982-83 the deficit rose from over $14 billion to over $27 billion, an increase of $13 billion in that one year.
People sometimes forget that our financial situation was out of control and that if these spending patterns had continued, we would have been $100 billion more in debt than we will be as a result of the measures we have introduced. It is necessary to remind Canadians that when we took office we said it was necessary to tackle the economic issues, including the deficit. I know that the first thing I am asked when I meet people in my riding is what we are doing to manage the economy and bring the deficit under control.
People are concerned about the future for their children and grandchildren if we simply keep piling up a debt without any thought about its implications in the future. For instance, 93 per cent of today's deficit is the result of paying interest on money borrowed to finance yesterday's deficit. We know that increasing the deficit at a rate that was out of control would inevitably lead to higher interest rates, a weakened dollar, and would have impaired our ability to maintain a wide range of programs. It would have potentially impaired our ability to provide the very social programs that we want for our elderly, our children and those in need.
We said two years ago that we would make changes. The House will recall that in the economic statement and our Budgets we laid out a program so that for the first time in 40 years government spending is actually reducing and, for the first time in six years, the deficit is also declining.
We are debating legislation which has increased revenues through sales taxes and excise taxes in certain areas. It is important to remember that while some taxes have increased,

November 3, 1986
Excise Tax Act
for every dollar in increased taxes, expenditures have been cut by $3.
Let us consider some of the steps that have been taken to reduce the deficit. It is never easy to cut programs and it causes some pain and hardship to those who may have a certain interest in certain government programs. However, we have had to take some tough action, including the elimination of the Canadian Home Insulation Program, the Registered Home Ownership Savings Program and Katimavik. We have closed down the heavy water plant, got rid of Canagrex and have modified the rate of indexation of transfer payments to the provinces. It is not easy to take these steps, but governing involves making some tough decisions. We know that each Department of government has been reviewed and is going through a process of managing more efficiently and spending smarter.
Hon. Members opposite may not want us to take these steps, but we feel it is in the public interest and what the people of Canada have asked us to do. There is no limitless pot of money from which we can draw and, if we do not make those very tough decisions, we cannot expect to maintain a competitive edge in the international field.
The measures we have implemented in the past two years include measures to reduce government expenditures and to sell off Crown corporations. Some of our measures have resulted in a reduction of $560 in the cost to average Canadian households.
The proof in the pudding is in the results of our measures, about which I am most pleased. No one can deny that job-creation has occurred in this country. Over one million more Canadians are working today than were working in September, 1984.1 indicated in my speech in reply to the Speech from the Throne that 80 per cent of those jobs are full-time. Members opposite keep giving other statistics but they cannot deny the truth.
We know that unemployment has decreased by 2.2 per cent between September, 1984 and September, 1986, so that it is now down to 9.5 per cent. Furthermore, we know that inflation is holding firm.
The Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) expressed some concern about the impact of these increased sales tax measures on the economy. We know that they have been in effect since April of this year and there has not been an adverse impact on employment which has, in fact, increased. We also know that consumer confidence has increased because consumer spending is at its highest level in 21 years and its second highest level in history. They have not had an adverse impact on consumer spending.
When we consider the international statistics, which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) quoted during the Throne Speech debate, we know that according to the 1986 report of the European Management Forum, in the past two years Canada has moved from eleventh place to sixth place in improving our competitive position. We can be very proud of
that record. Recently, a high level delegation from Japan visited Canada to meet the Government and private sector groups throughout the country. I had an opportunity to have an informal meeting with some of those delegates and discovered that they were almost astonished by the changes that have taken place in the economy of Canada in the past two years and the level of confidence that this was creating. Obviously, this will make Canada a much more positive place for investment and growth.
During the weekend the Prime Minister spoke to an organization and said that if we want to deal with the country's social problems, first we have to ensure that we have a healthy economy and economic growth. As he said: "Only a healthy economy can lead to the proper funding to combat social ills". It seems obvious, yet it is important that we reiterate those points time after time. It is always more pleasant to spend money. In fact, I find it interesting that the Liberals in their policy sessions being held across the country are saying: "Spend more money. Spend more money". That is all very nice, but we cannot afford to do that. When we spend more money in that way, ultimately it will come back to private citizens who will not then have the kind of income to invest in order to create the jobs which are required. It must always be balanced.
The particular increases with which we are dealing today are a very reasonable and sensible way to raise the 30 per cent which we believe should be raised through increases in taxation. There is a 1 per cent increase in excise tax in some areas. These changes will generate about $ 1 billion in additional revenue in 1987, which will really help us to meet our target of deficit reduction. At the same time, we have within this legislation looked at areas which need special attention. I recall when the Budget came down last April. I was particularly pleased by one of the measures which would exempt certain kinds of information for the travel industry from federal sales tax. That is information which is made available by Chambers of Commerce and Boards of Trade to help us sell Canada to tourists. That was one of the sensitive issues which we included in these provisions.
Hon. Members opposite have been concerned about the impact on lower income families, but they must keep in mind that in the enactment of the Budget we have indeed had that under consideration and have introduced a special refundable sales tax credit to lower income families. The credit provides $50 per adult and $25 per child, which could mean $100 per family with two children, and will be paid to families with an income of less than $15,000. The total benefits are reduced by $5 for every $100 in income over that amount. I think that particular measure, along with the measure we passed a couple of weeks ago for the refundable child tax credit, shows our concern about those families in Canada at the lower end of the wage scale. We know that many of those families are headed by women. We are trying to ensure that they benefit from the
November 3, 1986

measures and are not unduly burdened by tax increases. I believe we have accomplished that.
I think the measures we are discussing today, which were introduced in the Budget, fulfil all the criteria of our philosophy, our commitment to economic renewal which is based on more efficient management of Government, reducing Government spending and reducing the deficit, and only, when necessary, increasing taxes, and certain taxes in a way which has the least dampening effect on the economy or on the ability or the initiative of people to take risks and to create entrepreneurial activities and create jobs.
I was in Vancouver on Saturday and spoke at a fascinating conference of aboriginal women who were interested in going into business. There were 90 or 100 women from the Vancouver region who were all looking at opportunities to start new businesses. This conference helped them to develop skills and create the partnerships and the networks. I talked to many of those women. They had ideas for shops and child care services, on reserves and off reserves. There was a tremendous feeling of confidence and optimism. As we know, the majority of new jobs created in this country are created by small business. In British Columbia, women are creating small businesses twice as quickly as men.
We can think of the group I met and spoke with on Saturday as really the leading edge of what we want to see happen in this country; people taking risks, making investments, and we in Government providing them with the framework and the environment in which they can take those risks successfully. 1 felt so good about that particular experience that I wanted to share it with my colleagues.
I also feel good about the kind of legislation we are debating today because it is consistent with our over-all policy of economic renewal, of new opportunities for our citizens and, as we have always said, a new Canada for all Canadians.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT'S FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY-CONTRIBUTION TO WELLBEING OF SOCIETY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am honoured and privileged to point out that Transport Canada is celebrating its 50th anniversary today. I am sure that Hon. Members and all Canadians are as proud as all the employees of the Department to mark this first half century today, the first 50 years of Transport Canada's outstanding contribution to the well-being of our society.

Yesterday, November 2, was the fiftieth anniversary of the Department. On that day in 1936 the Department of Transport Act was proclaimed by Parliament when the former Departments of Marine, Railways and Canals, and the civil aviation branch of National Defence were merged into one.
Today Transport Canada's role and responsibilities are global in scope. Canadian airlines span the world. Search and rescue telecommunications are relayed through satellites. We must address environmental concerns and such issues as international terrorism in our planning.
I would like to salute Transport Canada and its people. May the next 50 years be as productive and inspiring as the last half century.

subsubtopic: DELAY IN PROCESSING RETURN OF STATUS APPLICATIONS
speechtext:

subsubtopic: DECREASE IN NUMBER OF LOW-INCOME PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, low-income Canadians are defined as those who spend more than 58.5 per cent of income on the essential items of food, clothing, and shelter. Happily, substantial progress against poverty has been made since the present Government took office. There were 298,000 fewer low-income Canadians in 1985 than there were in 1984.
The National Council on Welfare has pointed out two factors which account for this reduction. These are improved social program benefits and a reduction in unemployment. Obviously the major cause of poverty is unemployment and therefore the major weapon against it is job creation.
Since September, 1984, the Government has provided an economic climate in which over 600,000 jobs have been created and under which the unemployment rate has fallen from 11.7 per cent to 9.5 per cent.
The Government stands committed to alleviating the curse of poverty through the provision of long-term meaningful jobs for Canadians.

I would like to thank my colleague for Scarborough East (Mr. Hicks) for his very kind comments. Yes, indeed, the question of the air transportation tax is part of Bill C-14 which we have before us. To begin with, it is important to remember the reason for the air transportation tax. It is a tax which goes toward the provision of airport facilities and navigation services, so it is a tax directed toward specific services.
The Hon. Member will recall that prior to the introduction of the change in the last Budget, there was a transportation tax of 9 per cent without a ceiling. That was a hefty bill for people from the further regions of this country, particularly from the far North where the costs of air transportation can range from $800 to $1,000. What has been accomplished with the new revision is that the rate has gone from 9 per cent to 10 per cent but there is a ceiling of $50 on domestic travel. That means that even if the airfare is $1,000 from point A to point B, the limit of the transportation tax will be $50. That is certainly consistent with our whole approach in trying to make taxation fair. In this particular case it is going to help people who live in the far northern parts of the country or the farthest regions. On the other hand, there is not the same limitation on the tax which went into effect in August on the cost of air travel from outside the country. Generally speaking, you can get such good rates these days, and many of the airlines offer specials, that quite often you can go a long way for $500, which is where the $50 tax comes into effect.

Mr. Speaker, as we are having this debate, this measure is already in place, because it came into effect in April of this year. It might not harm for a moment to indicate to Canadians what is taking place in terms of a persecution of the consumer by way of increased sales tax. In most of these cases it is invisible because it is incorporated in the price of services or goods long before they reach the consumer.
What we are debating today with this Bill C-14 is an increase of 14 per cent in the sales tax for construction goods. This is an increase from 7 to 8 per cent in the tax rate applied to construction goods. There is an increase from 7 to 8 per cent in the cable and pay-TV services. There is an increase from 14 to 15 per cent in the tax rate as it applies to wine, beer, tobacco, and other alcoholic beverages. There is an increase in
the tax rate from 11 to 12 per cent in a number of other taxable goods, which are too numerous to be listed here today. However, the increase taking place now compared to the one which existed before translates into some pretty surprising percentages.
In the case of construction goods, the increase in the tax rate from 7 to 8 per cent means a percentage increase of 14 per cent in the tax itself. In the case of cable and pay-TV services, the increase as a result of this legislation represents an increase of 14 per cent. In the case of wine, beer, tobacco and other alcoholic beverages, it represents an increase of 7 per cent. The increase that applies on other taxable goods is an increase of 10 per cent.
On January 1 of this year we witnessed another increase in the tax rate on manufacturers' sales. At that time we had an increase comparable to what we are debating today. In other words, in the same year there is a double whammy by the Conservative Government to the Canadian consumer by way of applying twice an increase on sales taxes that in the end amounts to the following. There is an increase in the sales tax of 28 per cent on construction goods and similar material and an increase of 28 per cent in cable and pay-TV.
There was also an increase of 14 per cent on wine, beer, tobacco, and the like, as well as an increase of 10 per cent applied to all other taxable goods. If we look at the tax as it was before January 1 of this year and as it is now after two increases have taken place, we understand the decline in the political fortune of the Tories in Canada this year. We also understand why their performance in the polls is so weak, why there is a downward trend, and why their popularity in general is suffering.
We are witnessing a hard year in terms of the application of taxes upon consumers. It is a taxation regime based upon a Tory philosophy which says that everyone, no matter what their income, should pay the same tax. In addition, the tax is not visible at the time of purchases.
It is unlikely that the purchaser of construction goods will pay the tax in the end. It will be consumers at the retail level who will pay for it. In the case of cable and pay-TV services, the subscribers will pay for the increase in taxes. The same must be said about consumers of alcoholic beverages and tobacco. That is the inevitable conclusion at which one must arrive in examining the application of the measure before us for debate.
What is happening in 1986 is a continuing erosion of the purchasing power of consumers by way of the imposition of an invisible tax which hits harder those with lower incomes and much harder those who are below the poverty line. The policy is a typical Tory approach to economics. It reinforces the well known perception about which people on the street speak when they say that Tory times are tough times. It is another example of the application of economics which are regressive in social
November 3, 1986

terms and are bad per se because they diminish the capacity of consumers to purchase and to keep the economy healthful and vital.
Earlier this morning the Hon. Member for Lethbridge- Foothills (Mr. Thacker) made reference to the Bill as being a necessary instrument to pick up the tab for the deficit by taxation. That is the point of departure or the watershed between the Tory approach and the Liberal approach to tackling the deficit. The Tories are trying to tax people in every respect. They have the notion that by doing so the deficit will be reduced substantially. They say that it is a medicine which must be taken to reduce the deficit, the monster which has been described in various interventions on the part of the Conservative Party.
I submit that it is the wrong way in which to reduce the deficit. One does not bring down the deficit by applying a tax which hits the poor hardest and hits the well-to-do least. It is actually an unfair way of dealing with an important measure, that is, the reduction of the deficit. It should not be fought on the backs of those who can least afford it. In that respect Tory Members and those of us on this side of the House part ways in a very dramatic and drastic manner. I do not think they should pick up the tab for the deficit, as the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills put it, by way of taxation, particularly a sales tax which is applied equally on everyone and therefore hits hardest those who can cope the least.
There are other ways of reducing the deficit. There are other techniques of maintaining the good health of the economy, actually increasing its momentum, increasing the revenues of the state, and gradually coming to grips with a reduction in the deficit itself.
There is an aspect in Bill C-14 about which I should like to comment very briefly. It concerns the ways and means application on page 11a as it affects petroleum products, in particular regular gasoline, unleaded gasoline, and the like. We have the introduction of a tax whereby unleaded gasoline is taxed more heavily with the application of a tax of SO.0036 per litre and the tax on regular gasoline is $0.0032 per litre. In other words, we are witnessing the application of a policy whereby the consumer of unleaded gasoline, that is an individual driving an environmentally friendly type of engine, is being penalized by an ever-increasing tax on unleaded gasoline.
We on this side of the House raised this matter almost a year ago. At that time the Conservative Government had already introduced a taxation measure which applied a greater tax upon unleaded gasoline than upon regular gasoline. In second reading debate-and I believe it was also at third reading-we drew to the attention of the Government the way this could be avoided. We suggested that a tax increase on gasoline ought to be applied with greater emphasis on regular gasoline than upon unleaded gasoline in order to protect the environment. I remember Your Honour was in the Chair and
Excise Tax Act
listened patiently to what would be the advantages in environmental terms in the application of a greater tax on regular gasoline than on unleaded gasoline.
I regret to report that the Tories have done it again despite promises and statements made in public. For example, on October 31, 1985, as reported in The Globe and Mail, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. MacMillan) proclaimed that eliminating the price difference between leaded and unleaded gasoline might be the best way to end widespread misfuelling. He went on to say that he would co-operate with the federal Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and with provincial colleagues to see whether the disparities in the price of gasoline could not be addressed. Then he extolled about what Canadians ought to do, namely, pay a premium to protect our health. He indicated that this would be a way of protecting the health of our children.
As we know, unleaded gasoline is not as harmful to human health as is leaded gasoline. That was a year ago, almost to the day. However, we find ourselves facing a second increase. This despite representations made to the Government a year ago, and despite promises and declarations of good intentions, which is basically what they remain, by the Minister of the Environment. He seems to be very prone to making promises and impotent in delivering upon them. That is very regrettable because the question of taxation of unleaded versus regular gasoline is becoming a national concern. There is no reason why a Government which claims to be interested in protection of the environment, human health and other resources affected by acid rain, cannot proceed through a change in taxation policy to ensure that unleaded gasoline costs less at the pump than regular. I for one cannot understand why this cannot be achieved given the length of time which has gone by since the matter was first raised.
It is true other jurisdictions, being the provincial Governments, impose taxes on gasoline. It is my fervent hope that the Ontario Liberal Government will be the first jurisdiction to adopt a policy which taxes unleaded gasoline less than leaded. While that process is under way, however, we in this House of Commons have twice witnessed a tax Bill in which this basic fact has been ignored. Therefore I urge Conservative Members who care about the environment in fact as well as in words to register this point in their national caucus. The matter has not been dealt with. It is not right that the gap between leaded and unleaded gasoline would continue to rise to a difference of over 3 cents a litre at the pump. Imposition of the Ways and Means figure I mentioned earlier will result in an even greater differential.
I refer those Members concerned about the reaction of farmers to that excellent clause in this Bill which provides refunds to farmers on the purchase of gasoline. 1 refer now to Clause 9 as a whole which takes into account the desirability and necessity to compensate farmers, and I suppose it applies to fishermen as well, on the gasoline they consume.

November 3, 1986
Excise Tax Act
In essence this Government has to come to grips with its economic policy so as to make it jibe with its environmental policy. That has not yet taken place despite the repetitive promises made by the Minister of the Environment. In fact, the Government made a regressive decision by extending the phasing out of lead in gasoline to 1992 instead of 1990. For that reason alone let us at least have a tax policy which will result in a price for unleaded gasoline at the pump which is less than leaded.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure Canadians are not overjoyed today, listening to a parliamentary debate a proposed sales tax increase on certain products. No taxpayer in his right mind appreciates paying
more for any product, good or service he might consider buying.
Still, Mr. Speaker, Canadians readily admit that the existing situation could not last any longer. Canada was sliding down a dangerous hill, heading full speed for a bottomless pit. Under the previous Government, the gross national debt increased by 50 per cent in only a few years, and debt servicing soared by 85 per cent.
More specifically, the deficit rose from $14 billion to $27 billion between 1981-82 and 1982-83, almost doubling in a single year.
Mr. Speaker, we probably cannot repeat it too often.
Our annual budget is now $116 billion, and every time Canadian taxpayers are presented with a new Budget, they should realize that there will be a shortfall of nearly $30 billion-yes, $30 billion-in revenue to balance the budget, which means that we are spending more than we get in revenue. This shortfall is now $28 to $30 billion annually, but if we had not intervened, it would be as much as $38 to $40 billion annually, nearly $10 billion more per year. The annual deficit was close to $40 billion, as it was during the last year of the previous Government's term. This administrative disaster led us to apply sounder management practices aimed at reducing the rate of growth of the deficit, which we wanted to see below the growth rate of our economy.
The purpose of Bill C-14 is to achieve that goal through legislation that will generate revenu and at the same time reduce our expenditures. The tax increases produced in this Bill represent 30 per cent of our deficit reduction program, while spending cuts represent 70 per cent. Exactly what kind of revenue are we talking about in Bill C-14? Seven hundred million will be raised by increasing federal sales tax during the 1986 fiscal year, rising to $1.05 billion in 1987. Excise tax will produce $125 million in 1986, and twice that much: $250 million, in 1987.
However, there are other reasons as well for increasing our revenue and bringing down the deficit. Ninety-three per cent of the present deficit arises from interest payments on the amounts we borrow to finance the previous deficit. Yes, Mr. Speaker, 93 per cent of our present deficit consists of interest payments on the money we borrow to pay off the previous deficit.
We also want to maintain our basic social programs. Consider the child tax credit Canadian families will be able to claim this year. In fact, Canadians with incomes of less than $15,000 will be able to claim $300 per child in November. Furthermore, the child tax credit will be increased by $70, which will raise the credit to $524 starting next year.
Job-creation programs are also very important, and we are allocating $4 billion over two years to job creation through our six job-strategy programs.
November 3, 1986

Farmers will also benefit, Mr. Speaker, through a reduction in tax on the gas they use in their farm operations. This is the kind of assistance they need and the kind we are giving them.
Mr. Speaker, another very important measure, one we implemented in the last Budget, is the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption.
Mr. Speaker, 1 still remember that very recently some Canadian farmers told me how much they appreciate the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption. Mr. Blackburn, they said, you know, we were no longer even able to give or sell our farm to our children. It was viewed as a capital gain and we did not even have the money to pay taxes on it. Thanks to the tax reform-our tax reform-now we can do that, let our children take over and keep the farm going. This $500,000 capital gains tax exemption is a measure which Canadians really appreciate.
A number of other Government initiatives bear fruit as well, and this would be a good opportunity to raise the matter of employment. When we came into office the unemployment rate was 11.7 per cent, today it is down to something like 9.5 per cent. We have created 595,000 jobs since we took over in 1984, which works out to 24,792 jobs a month against 7,345 under the previous administration. In other words we are creating three to four times as many jobs each month. Three to four times as many jobs a month has to be some kind of an achievement, Mr. Speaker, a significant figure which Canadians should be aware of. It is still not enough, of course, what with an unemployment rate of 9.5 per cent, an improvement but still not enough by a long shot. We must keep up our efforts and, as a responsible Government, that is exactly what we are doing. We are always coming up with job-creation policies, ever on a quest for a fresh approach to this problem.
Mr. Speaker, Canada's economic growth is another challenging issue. In terms of economic growth, Canada ranks second among the 24 OECD member countries. It is indeed a promising performance. This means that, on 24 countries, Canada had the second best record for economic growth and job creation. That is an important factor and it must be taken into account.
Let us speak also about the announced tax reform. Our Government has said that it would examine the options offered for an in-depth tax reform. We remain committed to our objective of implementing a simpler, fairer and more efficient tax system. Our review deals with the relationships between the three major components of federal taxation, that is direct personal income tax, corporate income tax and the sales tax, and their role in meeting our tax reform objectives in Canada. Our Government has established major principles to promote the debate in coming months as well as public input on reform options. In fact, what we want is more equity in the tax system. Our taxation system must ensure an equitable distribution of the tax burden among all taxpayers. This means that taxpayers in the same situation must be covered by the same taxation system, that all high income individuals and all profitable corporations must pay their fair share of taxes and
Excise Tax Act
that similar products must be subject to the same sales tax rate. The sales tax burden must be distributed more equitably among goods and services and the sectors which produce them, which is not the case now.
When we talk about a tax reform, our objective is to reduce the personal tax rate and perhaps to increase the corporate tax rate. I refer to an article by reporter Vincent Cliche which appeared last October 29 in the newspaper Le Soleil. The author had this to say: Yet it has become necessary to review the method of taxation in Canada, first for a very pragmatic reason since the United States have already completed their own reform which will come into effect in 1988. The attraction of simplicity could incite many corporations or taxpayers in Canada to opt for the American system and to decide to pay their taxes in the United States. It is therefore important for us to join in this process. However, the major reasons for an indepth review of the tax system, as everyone including the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) himself recognizes, is that Canadian taxpayers pay too much in taxes, to the extent that the percentage of federal tax revenue from personal income tax has been increasing constantly in the last 25 years to reach the present figure of 50 per cent.
Finally, the tax burden balance between lower and higher income earners, between individuals and corporations, has been greatly jeopardized by the gradual introduction of tax shelters.
This is therefore a major tax reform, and I think that Canadians are happy to see our Government undertake such a reform.
While we are on the subject of Government policy, I should like to mention the one that was made public over the past weekend concerning a major contract which was awarded to Canadair for the maintenance of F-18 aircrafts. Mr. Speaker, there was a difference of less then 3 per cent between the Bristol Aerospace and Canadair. Our Government acted in Canada's best national interest when it decided to grant this contract to a Montreal corporation. I must say that even if this decision is difficult to accept for a province, I suggest that, under the circumstances, Canadair being an airplane manufacturer, it will fully benefit from this high technology transfer.
With this in mind, our Government decided to award a $104 million contract for three and a half years to Canadair. Over the weekend, a great many Canadians have congratulated our Government for its choice, a choice which was both difficult to make and of great importance in view of the high technology involved in this maintenance contract for F-18s.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps we should talk about the inflation rate, which is still around 4 per cent. This is part of this Government's performances, as is another one our policies applying to 185,000 widows and widowers aged 60 to 64, who can now get the spouse's benefit. This is very important.
There is of course something else that we might be able to implement and I am thinking in particular about single people who are in the same predicament and unfortunately cannot

benefit from it. In order to extend that, and of course I do not think there is one single Member here who would not wish we could give more to Canadian men and women in need or facing difficulty. But we need money for that, and it is not always possible to act as and when we would like to.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to recall that during the summer, when the Quebec Caucus met in the Beauce area, it was my pleasure as a Member for Jonquiere to present to my colleagues a working paper on voluntary retirement at age 60. This is another policy I know would be most popular with Canadian men and women. It would have the additional benefit of opening jobs for our young people who are looking for employment or are trying to get into the labour force after graduation, or for fathers or mothers aged over 40 who very often have difficulty re-entering the labour market.
Mr. Speaker, we now have 1,160,000 Canadian men and women aged 60 to 65, and I was recommending that gradually, over a five-year period, we implement a policy of voluntary retirement under which in 1988, for instance, people aged 64 could go on early retirement; in 1989, it would be those aged 63, in 1990 those aged 62, and so on and so forth. This would mean that Canadians who so desire, who have worked hard, could decide on a well-deserved retirement to allow young people who would like to work to get into the labour force. Mr. Speaker, it is a sad situation for Canadians, or for young people aged 20 to 25 to be jobless. And I can tell you that as Members of Parliament, we regularly have those people coming to our offices to discuss the problem. They would like us to introduce more measures to help young people get on the labour market and be entitled to a job, which is so rewarding for everyone.
Mr. Speaker, I mention that because it is important and it is part of this Government's policy, because we are trying to implement those policies, and in order of course to do that we need more revenues, and to make the Canadian economy work better and to continue reducing the deficit.
Bill C-14, the Bill we are considering today, has a disagreeable side for Canadians because we are going to increase sales tax in certain areas. People should realize that the money we raise in this way, $700 million this year and $1.05 billion next year, will enable us to sustain the social policies we are introducing now for the benefit of Canadians. I am sure they agree with what we are doing, Mr. Speaker, to put our economy on a sound basis and steer a straight course so that pretty soon, instead of an annual deficit of $30 billion, we will have a balanced budget within several years.
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank you for this opportunity to speak to Bill C-14 and the various sales tax increases it entails, and those were my comments on the subject.
