Member who just spoke indicated that the main reason for the establishment of Bill C-14 was to reduce the deficit and that the time is now. I do not believe anyone in this House does not recognize that the deficit is a major problem. We operate under a financial structure where our financial institutions are the strongest organizations in Canada and they will continue to take their pound of flesh regardless of the economics of the country and how much it hurts us. Therefore, we have to take seriously the fact that the deficit costs us $20 billion to $30 billion a year to service.
The point we should make clear as often as possible is that there are ways of dealing with the deficit other than nickel and diming us to death with sales taxes on every little item a consumer purchases. The sales tax in any form is a regressive tax. It takes the same amount of money away from persons who are trying to live on $7,000 or $10,000 a year as it does from the person who earns $100,000 a year. Since we all consume approximately the same amount of most items, this is not a fair way of dividing the burden. All Parties in this House and every Government in Canada has recognized that there is some value in having a progressive type of tax. But that progressiveness is being attacked by the Government with the Bill which is before us today. Progressive taxation means that the person who is able to pay the most, pays the most. A regressive tax is a tax which it is necessary for the individual to pay regardless of how much he earns. Therefore, every time tax is put on a loaf of bread, whether the bread is purchased by someone on welfare or someone who receives a very small wage, they will have to pay the seven cents, eight cents or nine cents, whatever the tax amounts to on that loaf of bread, in the same way as a person who earns $100,000. Of course, that tax affects the low wage earner a great deal more than it does someone who earns a good wage.
It seems to me that when the Government uses these sales taxes, these hidden taxes, to a large extent, in its attempt to reduce the deficit, it is being cowardly in its approach. It is unwilling to say to those who earn a great deal of money that they should pay. It chooses instead to hide the tax so that everything which is purchased will contribute to the reduction of the deficit. The Government thinks this will not be noticed by most individuals because when one goes to buy a loaf of
Excise Tax Act
bread, the fact that it is two cents or three cents more expensive will not really be a factor because that loaf of bread will still be purchased.
It is of great concern to me, to members of my Party and to many people across the country that this Bill deals not with who is able to pay but only with the collecting of money. It does not recognize that Governments have a social responsibility to even out the amount of money which people live on.
Two weeks ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) rose in his place and promised he would make some changes in the taxation structure to make it more progressive and fairer for ordinary Canadians. But today we are debating a Bill which does exactly the opposite. This Bill is not fair to ordinary Canadians and will make it more difficult for the Canadian family to survive. What makes it more of a problem is the fact that the Government has shown that this is not something new it thought up last week. This is a policy which it has carried on for two years and intends to continue to carry on. In the first two years of this Conservative Government, instead of introducing a fairer taxation system, it has increased the amount of taxes to be paid. It has made the system less fair than it was before. There were quite a few problems in the tax system before the Government came to power but instead of doing what it said it was going to do in its campaign speeches before it was elected, it has continued to increase the complexity and the unfairness of the tax system. The Government in the two years it has been in power has added something over $800 per family in direct taxes. It has also added a considerable amount in regular income taxes. So that a family of four who thought they were doing pretty well two years ago, unless they received a 7 per cent increase in income per year, is earning less today. That problem is being perpetuated by this particular Bill.
The Government has a propensity for using hidden taxes. Sixty-nine per cent of the tax increases in the last two years have been in excise and sales taxes and only 31 per cent of the increase of money taken in has been in income tax. The Government suggests there are a lot more people earning a better wage than before, at least it keeps telling us that. I think it is important to recognize that the Government is speaking from a certain position. It is likely to continue to develop its tax structure in that way regardless of how much it says it will improve it.
We have suggested that the Government increase the corporate tax rate. I was not surprised to hear the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) defend the corporate tax structure-the Liberal Party has been doing that for many years. The Government is now suggesting that it will increase corporate taxes. The Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) seemed to express some concern with respect to that point. We must recognize that if corporate taxes are increased it is likely that there will be some adjustments passed on to consumers. Tax on corporations is tax on income which

November 3, 1986
Excise Tax Act
cannot be avoided in quite the same way that other taxes can be avoided. If a corporation makes more money by gouging the consumer then it will have to pay more tax on the extra money it earns. We recognize that this extra money may be used to increase profits. If that happens then a law which is in place in the country will have to be utilized when it is obvious that corporations are gouging consumers.
The Minister of Finance has suggested that what the Government will do is to close the loopholes and eliminate some of the tax expenditures which the Auditor General suggests costs the Government some $28 billion per year. If this is done, the Government will be able to take advantage of this forgone money and increase the income of the Government. Consequently, it can do what it spends so much time telling us it will do, that is, reduce the deficit.
Today I had the fortunate-or unfortunate-adventure of looking into what is happening to the farm community in Saskatchewan. As Hon. Members know, the Government in the last year established the Farm Debt Review Board. Maybe it has not helped the farmers much as yet. There is even some suggestion that it may not help farmers. However, it has done one thing. It has made available statistics about farm foreclosures. For instance, statistics from the Farm Debt Review Board, which is in place in every province, show that there were 1,233 notices by financial institutions of intention to foreclose against farms in Canada between August 5 and October 16, a matter of just over two months. I was a little shocked to find out that Saskatchewan accounted for 677 of those notices. In other words, more than one-half of those notices were filed in the Province of Saskatchewan. The rest of the country is also in bad shape. For instance, Alberta had 217 financial organizations file against farmers. Manitoba had 110; Ontario had 142; Quebec had 42; and there were 27 in New Brunswick. Little Prince Edward Island even had 12 financial organizations file against farmers. The same is true in the case of British Columbia.
I make the point that even as the Government puts in place what it says may help farmers, it brings in this Bill which affects every item a farmer buys. It affects every item which is necessary for production. Today farmers will tell us that it is input costs which are killing them. I refer to the cost of fuel, the cost of money, fertilizer and chemicals. These are costs which are making farming less profitable when one considers the low prices farmers receive for the commodities which they produce. The Government talks about how it will help the farmer through the review board and other measures while at the same time it puts forward a Bill such as this which will cost the farmer even more money. I use farming as an example, but this measure will affect every industry in the same way. Each time direct taxes are increased input costs are increased. This in turn makes it more difficult for industries to make profits.
Over the last few years the effect of increasing input costs without increasing commodity values has decreased farm incomes to the extent that there have been 1,233 filings with respect to foreclosures in a matter of a few months. That is
only a small part of what will happen to the farming community. I suggest that what the Minister of Finance is doing through this measure is playing a shell game with the taxpayers. He is telling them that he will shift the tax burden and reduce the amount of income tax they must pay. Taxes may disappear momentarily, but in the end they will return in larger amounts than ever before.
Instead of this shell game which moves taxes from income to direct taxes the approach should be much more worth-while. If the Government continues in this approach it will not be long before we will be penalizing the poor and ordinary Canadians to the extent that we will be paying much more in terms of welfare. We will be increasing the number of food banks necessary to keep people alive. The taxation process that is being put into effect through this Bill will contribute to this.
I believe the direction that is being taken is wrong. Instead of trying to increase direct taxation, the Government should take the advice of the Auditor General and eliminate as quickly as possible tax expenditures from corporations.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak on this Bill. A number of Hon. Members have spoken about what the Bill is about and what it is not about. If I may, I would like to discuss what the Bill attempts to do and why it attempts to do it. Then, since members of the other Parties have raised a number of questions about social policy, I would like to spend most of my time speaking about what we have done in that area of great importance to many Canadians.
Some Hon. Members say that it does not contain too much good news, but the good news in the Bill is that it provides a one-year extension of the fuel tax rebate for primary producers. The rebate will go from three cents per litre to 3.5 cents per litre. We believe that is important in that it fulfils a commitment made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to the primary producer sector which, as you know, Mr. Speaker, is in great difficulty.
The Bill is designed to raise revenue. We are chronically short of revenue thanks to the 15 or 16 years of financial mismanagement on the part of the earlier Government. The Bill will generate approximately $700 million in the present fiscal year and about $1 billion in 1987.
It is a little known fact that about 93 per cent of today's deficit has accrued as a result of paying interest on money borrowed to finance the previous Government's accumulated deficits. That, of course, has led to higher interest rates. Interest rates are decreasing, but they are not low enough yet. The deficit has led to a weaker dollar, and I would point out that about $90 billion is owed by Canadian provincial Governments, the federal Government, Crown corporations, private citizens and corporations to external creditors.
Maintaining a strong dollar and keeping interest rates as low as possible are two things which are very important to Canadian men, women and children. The national debt is close to $250 billion. The mountain of red ink in which we find ourselves impairs our ability to provide better and richer social
Excise Tax Act
programs to citizens who need them. We are trying to spend smarter. We are trying to eliminate waste and unnecessary programs. We are trying to sell off some Crown corporations and we are trying to help low-income Canadians.
I believe our social programs are excellent. Someone has said that a rising tide lifts all boats including human boats. The creation of jobs is probably the most important social policy we can have. We have created fully 595,000 jobs since we were elected in the 1984 election. The national unemployment rate was 11.7 per cent on election day. I am happy to confirm that last month, it was 9.5 per cent. I know, as do other Members from western Canada and the Maritimes, that the unemployment rate is still too high in our own regions but over-all, jobs are being created at an average rate of about
25,000	per month.
More than 75 per cent of the jobs that have been created since we took office are full-time jobs. Youth unemployment nationally has dropped by fully 112,000 since the election or, in percentage terms, from a dreadful 18.4 per cent to about 15 per cent. Of course, it must still drop further.
Fully 328,000 more women across Canada were working last month than in September 1984. The unemployment rate for women across Canada has dropped from 12 per cent at the time of the election to 9.7 per cent now. I understand that employment has increased and unemployment has decreased in all 10 provinces since the election. This is small comfort to an unemployed constituent of yours or mine. While door-knocking about 10 days ago, I met a person from the oil sector whose income had dropped from a salary of $4,000 a month to $1,000 a month in unemployment insurance benefit. That is a very difficult thing for him to go through. He, you, and I are all grateful for the unemployment insurance safety net.
My point in citing these figures is that creating a social, business, and investment climate where jobs can be created is a central feature of our social strategy on this side of the House. More jobs are still needed, especially in the west, Quebec, and Atlantic Canada. Unlike our political opponents, we have already shown considerable success in creating a climate where jobs are being created in good numbers. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Jonquiere (Mr. Blackburn) mentioned that the OECD forecast that this year Canada will have the best employment growth rate of any major industrialized country of the 24 OECD countries. It is this political Party on this side of the House more than any other that cherishes the inherent dignity and worth of each individual Canadian. Our Party does not look at our fellow citizens as being members of this consumer group or that production unit. We see people as individuals created by a creator who must never again be treated by Government as objects, units of production, or the like. From that perspective comes true compassion and help for disadvantaged Canadians.
Let me illustrate what we have already achieved in three areas. First, with regard to disabled persons, there has been a

November 3, 1986
Excise Tax Act
substantive increase in funding for the participation program which encourages self-reliance, self-determination, and self-managment by disabled Canadians. The Walter Dinsdale Information Centre for Disabled Persons opened in Calgary in April, 1986. There were new measures designed to improve access for disabled individuals to federal Government buildings. There was an increase in the maximum housing renovations program for the disabled to $5,000 from $1,500. There was a significant broadening of the definition of "disabled person" in the Income Tax Act for purposes of eligibility for the $2,590 disability deduction, which is expected to add about
120,000	disabled persons to the current claimants. I am very proud of that record for disabled Canadians.
Second, with regard to seniors, we have extended the spouse's allowance to more than 85,000 low-income widowed persons who are mostly women, aged 60 to 64, regardless of the age of their spouse at the time of death. We have significantly enhanced pension and other benefits to our veterans and their spouses. Pension plans in federally-regulated sectors are to be improved by our legislation on such issues as portability, benefits for part-time employees, and equal benefits for men and women. Proposed changes to the Canada Pension Plan will improve it in terms of its future financial health, benefit elibility as early as age 60, increased disability benefits and the continuation of survivor benefits upon remarriage. Many seniors will benefit from our new definitions of "disability" for purposes of the Income Tax Act. A further 350,000 senior taxpayers have been exempted from having to make more tax instalment payments. Thank goodness for that. We have increased flexibility in using funds accumulated in RRSPs and removed the maximum limit on registered retirement income funds. We have funded over 1,900 New Horizon Program projects in one year alone.
Third, with regard to women and families, about 10 days ago in the House we debated our child tax credit proposal, under which will hopefully next month send a prepayment of $300 per child to approximately 700,000 families whose income in 1985 was $15,000 or less. More than 4 million families with incomes of less than $15,000 will also receive a refundable sales tax credit of $50 for each adult and $25 for each child.
We are committed to economic and social equality for women. The latest issue of Chatelaine magazine provides a pretty fair assessment of some of our initiatives. More is needed, but we are making headway in some important areas. The recent Throne Speech outlined a number of initiatives to protect and enhance Canadian families, which are the cornerstone of our society. Unfortunately, they are probably more under attack now than at any point in Canadian history. We will move on pornography. This is simply hate literature against women, children, and the family. Its linkage to increased crimes against women and children is pretty clear. Robert Lunney, our Police Chief in Edmonton recently pointed out that you can obtain video tapes in Edmonton which
advocate incest. Is it any wonder that there were a reported
17,000	sexual assaults in 1985 alone across Canada?
For the first time in history, we will initiate a national drug strategy against illegal drugs. Can anyone in the House doubt that a $9 billion to $10 billion a year illegal drug industry is at the epidemic level? I note that, as was mentioned earlier in Question Period, according to Dr. Gallup about 75 per cent of Canadians think that it is at the epidemic level, as was pointed out by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
We have already moved against street soliciting, primarily because of the Hutt decision which in effect said that it is virtually impossible to be found guilty of soliciting in a public place. This created many juvenile prostitutes of both sexes. Once the new law is finally upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada, which I am certain will be the case, it will reduce the number of young boys and girls who enter this self-destructive and brutal occupation.
In short, we believe that deeds are more important than words in matters of social policy. We have already done much. We will do a great deal more. The Bill itself before the House is part of a mosaic of raising more money to enable us to do more things to help Canadians in distress and in difficulty to cope with problems that they need help with.

speechtext:
It gives me great pleasure to rise this afternoon to address the House of Commons on Bill C-14, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act.
I listened with great pleasure to the speaker before me who was representing the Government side on this particular piece of legislation. Perhaps it conjures up comments made by a colleague of his. I used the past tense because he is no longer a member of the Conservative Party or the governing Party. He is the Member of Parliament for Terrebonne (Mr. Toupin), who now sits as an independent. One of the many reasons that Member of Parliament prefers the independent category as opposed to the Party of the governing side is that, in his own words, he believes that the Conservative Government is essentially a Party of the rich, a Party very much interested in the elitist category of this country and not a Party of the people. Using his own definition, he felt that he and his principles and the values represented in his riding precluded him, and perhaps impelled him, not to sit as a member of the Government Party but to seek his independent category and thus better represent the aspirations of his own constituents.
When you look at Bill C-14 you see the facts behind the reasons for the Member of Parliament for Terrebone and the very difficult decision that he must have had in switching from the governing side to that of independency. Bill C-14 states that the federal manufacturers' sales tax increas on construction goods goes up from 7 to 8 per cent. On cable and pay-TV services it goes up from 7 to 8 per cent. On alcoholic beverages and tobacco there is a rise from 14 to 15 per cent. On other goods there is a rise from 11 to 12 per cent. There is an alcohol and tobacco excise tax, as I earlier indicated. There is an airport transportation tax. There is a telecommunication
November 3, 1986

program service tax. There is a motive fuels tax. And on and on.
Basically, Canadian citizens are not advocating that taxes should be going down. All Canadians, including Members of the House, know that if taxes are to go anywhere, they will go up, or remain the same. That principle is accepted by Canadians from the Atlantic to the Pacific as long as the tax burden is fair and equitable and as long as taxes are applied in a way Canadians can accept. Canadians must know that they are being asked to shoulder expenses incurred by a federal Government which wishes to do well for the citizenry across the land. Canadians accept that principle if all taxpayers are being asked to shoulder the same burden, proportionately speaking. However, there is great concern about the philosophy of the Conservative Government that some people should pick up a bigger piece of the tax burden. Some individuals are being asked to shoulder disproportionately the burden of taxes.
This gives rise to the reality that there is a growing disparity between the rich and the poor, a growing gulf between the have and the have-nots, a growing gulf between those in the urban centres and those in the more regionalized and perhaps disadvantaged areas. This fuels speculation that somehow the priorities of the Government are out of whack and that the burden being asked of those less well off is unfair and inequitable. It is at that point that the Government is asking for trouble. It is aggravating an already bad situation, and it is really trying to kick the poor taxpayer who cannot bear another kick. That is when we have a tax revolt; that is when the fires of disparity give rise to emotionalism.
Individual taxpayers cannot be asked to carry the burden unfairly. When we look at unfairness, what are we talking about? Let us look at the last couple of Budgets introduced by the Government. We see an unfairness in the cumulative tax increases. A family with an income in the range of $15,000 to $20,000 will be facing a cumulative tax increase of some 23 per cent by 1990, compared with a 15 per cent increase being faced by those earning between $30,000 and $50,000, a 4 per cent increase being faced by those earning $100,000, and a 2 per cent increase being faced by those earning $200,000. What do we think a $15,000 wage earner will do? What questions will he or she be asking of elected representatives, more specifically of the Government of the day? One does not have to be an economist to understand the frustrations being felt by such individuals. That is where the disparity or the fuel for enhancing the disparity comes in.
They are asking a $15,000 wage earner to face a 23 per cent increase by 1990. On the other hand, the $200,000 wage earner will only face a 2 per cent increase. The $15,000 wage earner will not take it sitting down. He or she will send a message to the Government, as we are trying to do in this national Chamber. We, as Members of Parliament, have an obligation to rise and at least inform the Government of what its financial and fiscal policies are doing across the land,
Excise Tax Act
particularly in communities like York West that are typical working-class and middle-class communities.
I have attended numerous public meetings on the subject of taxes and the fiscal policies of the Government. No one in the country minds meeting together our fiscal challenges in the 1990s and beyond. However, no one is prepared to shoulder the burden on an unfair basis.
The disparities between the have and the have-nots or the rich and the poor are actually being reflected for the very first time in national polling studies. Never before have Canadians perceived the gulf of disparity to be hitting Canada as much as it has in the last few years. They never perceived Canada as having a well defined class structure. Although we have Mr. Porter's vertical mosaic, Canadians did not want to believe that there was a well defined class structure. For the first time in history there are very clear signals from polling studies that Canadians are beginning to understand and accept the perception of class disparities or class structures.
The fights in our country have been along other lines. We have had linguistic battles between the legitimate rights of Francophones and other communities which perhaps did not wish to extend those rights across the board. We have been able to put that behind us, for the most part. We have had struggles between the East and the West, where perhaps regionalism gave rise to emotionalism, where perhaps Alberta could not understand the manufacturing centre of Ontario and vice-versa. We have also had struggles among provincial Governments whose responsibility it is to protect their regions and parochial concerns, as well as the clashes which have ensued with the federal Government. Those facts tell us that the country is not easy to manage or to govern because of its vastness in size and what size implies in terms of priorities.
However, we have never had the battles along the lines of class structures which have unfortunately occurred in other parts of the world such as Great Britain. Those fires have been fuelled consistently for years under Margaret Thatcher and her brand of Conservatism. We are beginning to see an element of that disparity taking on a more active role.
Is it any wonder that we see the manifestation of those disparities and inequities indicating that somewhere in the system things are not right? When we look at the increases in the numbers of food banks in the country, we realize that something is wrong. Not only are there increases in the numbers of food banks, whether they are in local parishes or in community centres in Vancouver, Toronto or Montreal, regrettably and unfortunately the line-ups outside food banks are growing longer and the food supplies in those banks are becoming more sparse. Is it any wonder there was a conference on food banks and the hungry in Toronto this past weekend?
We are in 1986; we are not in the 1940s. There is nothing more degrading for human beings in society than having to line up in the morning with their children in tow to ask for their piece of daily bread. There is nothing more serious than

human beings having to say to the state, society, their neighbours, community centres, or local parishes: "I do not have enough dollars to go to the IGA to buy food for my supper this evening". Thousands of individuals are lining up in front of food banks. I have seen them in Toronto and I have seen them in Vancouver. There is nothing more repugnant than to have to see that. There is nothing more repugnant than to have to ask ourselves why in today's rich, educated, technological society we witness fellow Canadians having to line up at food banks. Yet, when you look at something like Bill C-14, it is not surprising at all.
Consider some of the statistics produced by that very Government. After all these cumulative tax measures are in place, a person earning $50,000 or more faces a 1.2 per cent increase in taxes by the end of 1986. Yet a single parent family with two children faces a 2.1 per cent increase. At the very least the single parent family would expect the numbers to be reversed. Someone with a $100,000 income will pay a tax increase of 1.7 per cent. However, an elderly couple with less than $25,000 has a 2 per cent increase. Is it any wonder that the National Council on Welfare put out a report just last month which said the disparity between rich and poor in Canada is increasing at an alarming rate?
It said there were close to 4 million Canadians, or 16 per cent of our population, living in poverty. That is more than there were in 1980. One child in five is growing up in poverty, single mothers are five times more likely to be poor, and 60 per cent of female single parent families are poor. If that is the unfortunate reality facing Canadians from coast to coast, then why do we not have legislation which will adequately address that reality? Why are we asking the elderly to pay more than the $100,000 wage-earner? Why is the cumulative tax about 23 per cent for those earning $15,000, and only 4 per cent for those earning $100,000?
I would suggest, and other Canadians would suggest, that somehow the Government has its priorities out of whack. Somehow the mind-set governing its philosophy is out of whack with the realities. If there are 4 million poor, if tax increases are more for those less well off, then we are not talking about fairness and equity. We are proving the truth of the words of the Hon. Member for Terrebonne when he described the philosophy which has enveloped the Conservative Party and the Government of Canada.
We are not talking only about the working poor. We are also talking about a middle class which has constantly and consistently been clobbered by the Government. An individual came to my office last Saturday during constituency day and said he always thought of himself as a member of the middle class. He has a bungalow, two children, his wife works parttime and he holds down a pretty good job. What he then said was very indicative of where people are coming from in their thinking about a Government of the stripe we have seen over the last two years. He said the Government is making it more
difficult for him to call himself a member of the middle class. That individual and thousands of others like him are beginning to see society in terms of the politics of extremism.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to continue debate on Bill C-14, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act. This Bill provides for the third increase by the Government in the sales tax and excise tax since it took power in September of 1984. We sometimes leave the impression that the tax increases are much smaller than they actually are because we talk about a 1 per cent increase. To be more accurate, we should be describing it as an increase of one percentage point in the tax base. These seemingly small one percentage point increases mount up to a great deal of tax. One should consider this not as an increase of 1 per cent on three different occasions, but as a basic sales tax increase to 8 per cent from the 5 per cent sales tax when the Government took power. That is an increase of over 40 per cent, which reflects a much greater increase than 1 per cent.
Those 1 per cent increases have added up. In 1982, federal revenues from excise taxes and duties amounted to just over $2 billion. This year they will total more than $4 billion on an annual basis and will be in excess of between $5 billion and $6 billion per annum going into 1988. This means there is nearly a 300 per cent increase in that type of tax over the mandate of the Government.
We know that the 1984 Economic Statement contained an agreement by the Conservatives to increase federal sales taxes which had been announced by the Liberals. It also contained an increase of a percentage point for federal sales tax, bringing it from 5 per cent to 6 per cent, and an increase in the petroleum compensation charge. Just over six months later, in the May 1985 Budget, there was a further 1 per cent increase in sales tax, to 7 per cent. As a result of the February Budget and the implementation of this Bill, there will be a further 1 per cent increase in sales tax on April 1, bringing the sales tax on these items to 8 per cent from the 5 per cent in September, 1984. In a matter of two years, sales tax has risen from 5 per cent to 8 per cent. In addition, this legislation will increase taxes on certain goods from 11 per cent to 12 per cent, and from 14 per cent to 15 per cent on wine and spirits.
This Bill does not reflect small increases of 1 per cent, but very substantial increases in excess of 10 per cent to sales and excise taxes in this country. These extreme increases add up very quickly as far as individual Canadians are concerned.
To this point the Conservatives have netted the federal coffers almost $7 billion from increased sales and excise taxes alone. During the same period, the Progressive Conservative Government has increased corporate income taxes by an additional $ 1.4 billion and has increased personal income taxes by $3.3 billion. This amounts to a total tax grab of more than $11.5 billion since coming to power just over two years ago. If
it were not so serious it would be rather amusing to consider that the Government has attempted to reduce the deficit by increasing these taxes between $11 billion and $12 billion, yet the deficit has only decreased by a few billion dollars on an annual basis.
In the year the Government took office the deficit exceeded $36 billion. This year the deficit will be over $30 billion even though the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) promised to reduce the deficit to below that amount. The Government has not succeeded in bringing down the deficit by as much as it has charged Canadians in extra taxes.
There have been some serious cuts to services and additional charges have been made against Canadians who use Government services. Yet no dent as such has been made to the deficit. I believe the accumulated deficit is approaching some $300 billion, and while it costs a great deal to carry this deficit the only changes the Government seems capable of making are increases that will affect ordinary Canadians by reducing their take-home pay and purchasing power.
Several high profile groups in Canada hqve commented on this reduction in purchasing power. They include the National Council on Welfare, which is often quoted by my Party. It has noted that there has been a steady decline in disposable income of all Canadians, which can be expected to continue over the next five years as a result of this kind of taxation policy we see in Bill C-14. It is essentially a regressive tax because it taxes the items that people need, like goods and services to maintain their standard of living. This is a hidden tax because it is already included in the purchase price of goods. On the other hand, provincial sales taxes are very clear because when one pays the bill, the additional 5 per cent or 7 per cent is clearly stated as the extra sales tax. Similarly, we know what we pay in income tax.
Income tax in Canada is considered to be a progressive tax because the rate of income tax increases as one's taxable income goes up. This means that people who have $20,000 in taxable income will pay a lower proportion in income tax than those who have a taxable income of $45,000. I believe the rationale behind this tax is good because it assumes that there are certain goods and services that all of us must have and on which we cannot cut back. We need a certain minimum for food, clothing, housing and transportation needs in this country to maintain a certain standard of living. Families who are in the $20,000 income range do not have much opportunity to save, but families who earn $45,000 find it much easier to set aside savings or pay a higher tax rate. Therefore, our system of taxation is a progressive system in which higher income families are charged more.
However, our over-all tax policy has not been so clear or fair. We have permitted the income tax system to deteriorate over the years to the point where it is reported that some corporations pay absolutely no income tax even though they showed very good profits. We have seen statistics made public in the last few months that show that some 80,000 Canadian
November 3, 1986

corporations, all of which showed substantial profits, paid absolutely nothing in corporate income tax.
This is the way we have permitted our income tax system to deteriorate. We have moved away from a progressive form of taxation to one which is now so full of loopholes that, to some extent, it is becoming a regressive kind of tax. Families with an income of $20,000 are paying more tax than some corporations which in the past year earned profits of up to $450 million. These corporations paid absolutely zero in income tax. That does not seem fair when a family is trying to struggle along with an income of just over $20,000 and is not receiving any tax breaks. That family pays its share of income tax, but one of our large corporations in the downtown area showed hundreds of millions of dollars of profits and contributed absolutely nothing by way of income tax to the maintenance of our services.
The two views of taxation are whether it should be a progressive tax or a regressive tax. The arguments some Conservative philosophers have given is that the regressive tax is in fact a fair tax. We have heard some allusions to that, although not too many Government Members, to their credit, have actually defended regressive taxation. They have made references to regressive taxation and supported that position in a vague sort of way by saying: "When the tide rises, it carries us all, rich and poor alike". But they know in fact it carries the very wealthy much further and much faster than it carries the low income earner.
The continued move is toward the hidden regressive kind of sales tax that we see presented in this legislation before us today. This is the third attempt at this kind of legislation. What the Government has succeeded in foisting on the people of Canada, has resulted in less income for ordinary Canadians and a rapidly accelerated tax load. For those people who are considered middle income earners, who may have both spouses working, two dependent children and a family income of $35,000, a fairly typical Canadian family, these particular sales tax and excise tax increases which have come into effect since the Government took over, have resulted in a total increase in taxation to that family of just over $1,300.
The 1984 Economic Statement which placed the first one per centage point increase on sales tax cost that family approximately $350 a year in clothing and building materials and so on which would include the hidden sales tax. The Budget of May, 1985 added another $325 to that family's tax burden. The recent February Budget which announced the sales tax and excise tax increase we are debating today, will have added another $170 per year. These increases total just over $1,300 for this particular family, and $845 of this new burden would be due to sales taxes. The rest would be the increases in excise taxes mostly with regard to transportion costs, driving one's automobile or riding the bus. With the increase in fuel tax and airport taxes, the increase in airline
Excise Tax Act
tickets would show up in that family's expenditures if they took a vacation once during that period of time.
The tax increases are fairly substantial. Most Canadians have not been so privileged as to have received that kind of income increase to their own personal family income. As a result of this kind of tax policy, low income and medium income families are worse off. Government Members have made it very clear that there is a tax credit for those low income families who earn between $10,000 and $15,000. We applaud that, but we also point out it is very hard going in the very cold waters of "sink or swim" for those families who earn between $15,000 and $20,000. Their income position is not a whole lot better but they do not have that kind of tax break. They still pay the extra excise and sales tax with no compensation back in the form of a tax break. Those families are finding it increasingly difficult to live under this kind of tax regime. These hidden taxes are not just sales taxes. I mentioned so far the increases to sales tax. I would like to talk a little bit about the kinds of increases which have fallen on Canadians who use fuel. This is something which is important because Canada is a large country and we must have fuel not only for heating our homes but to be able to move around in our automobiles and use our transportation system. There was an increase of two cents a litre on September 3, 1985. There was a further one cent per litre increase on January 1, 1986. There has been a new excise tax of two cents per litre on diesel and aviation fuel imposed since that time. Those increases have meant extra costs to the budgets of ordinary families with no recognition of how much harm that is doing. The Government simply explains it away by saying: "This is the way we are asking our people to fight against the large deficit". Yet the Minister, who has collected something in the neighbourhood of $11 billion and $12 billion in new and extra taxes in the sales and excise area alone, has, in spite of cuts, still left us with an annual budgetary deficit not very much different from the annual budgetary deficit left to us by the Liberals. With a total expenditure of something over $120 billion annually, we are failing to collect taxes in excess of $30 billion. The Government has not decided to collect taxes from large corporations where the money is available but has chosen instead to go after low and middle income earners. It is ignoring the several hundred millions of dollars of profits of corporations which are escaping without paying any taxes at all. This is unfair. The situation must be but right. There is a great deal of money to be collected from that area.
One of the old rules of taxation Tommy Douglas used to follow when he was Premier of Saskatchewan-and I would point out he got rid of what was for his time the very large deficit he inherited-was to give tax breaks to the ordinary people in Saskatchewan and taxing those corporations which had surplus funds. Failure to do that will result in a continuation of the kind of policies we had under the Liberals where these large tax breaks have resulted in large amounts of money in corporate coffers. These corporations do not use this money to start new businesses. They simply use them to buy each

Budget directly on the taxpayers in the form of sales and excise taxes, are in fact a form of direct taxation of poor people and those who can least afford to pay. Quite sincerely, this particular tax measure encapsulates the philosophy of the Conservative Party. I hesitate to say Progressive Conservative Party because I think it is a contradiction in terms, a contradiction underlined by the kind of regressive tax measures introduced by Bill C-14 and further compounded by recent statements made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) relating to tax reform.
The Minister has been titillating the Canadian public for quite some time. He has been suggesting that he will introduce a tax reform package that will in fact ease the burden currently faced by middle-class families. We realize, because of the announcement he made in the House a few days ago, that the Minister is not prepared to ease the burden on middle income taxpayers. Sure, he will reduce personal income taxes, but at the same time he is suggesting that we charge more sales taxes and more of the kind of direct taxation which hits the hardest at those who are in the worst position to pay.
Let us look at the effect of the tax measures contained in Bill C-14 along with sales tax and other tax measures. It has become increasingly clear that the Government has no intention of easing the tax burden on those who cannot afford to pay. In fact, Government Members seem to have devoted themselves primarily to those who cannot afford to pay. An elderly couple earning a total of $27,000 per year-and most Hon. Members will know that senior citizen couples do not, generally speaking, earn that much-will face a total tax increase of $500. At the same time, a family of four earning $100,000 will face a tax increase of $1,740. The percentage of the tax increase imposed on the elderly couple earning $27,000 per year is higher than the percentage of the tax increase imposed on the family earning $100,000 per year.
The same is true all the way down the line. The group that is hardest hit by Tory fiscal policies aimed at ordinary working people is the family with one income earner who has one adult dependent and two children. Because of measures introduced in the last three Budgets, that kind of family will pay an extra $630 in taxes, an increase of 2.1 per cent. In my own community, a steelworker who may be supporting a wife and a couple of children on $30,000 per year will be asked to bear a greater burden of the public tax increases than a family of four earning $100,000 per year. The vice-president of the steel company who may be earning $100,000 per year or more will be faced with less of an increase in his or her taxes than the average steelworker. I think this is what is intrinsically wrong with Bill C-14 and with the legislation that we have seen over the last couple of years. However, if we are talking about a family whose annual income amounts to $30,000, all indicators in Canada show that a man with a wife and two children who earns only $30,000 a year will see his tax rate go up by 2.1 per cent, or $630 more per family.
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the Conservative Government policy is to have middle and even low income families pick up the tab.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the response of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is that families earning less than $15,000 are entitled to a rebate. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is shameful and utterly ridiculous to brag about rebates to families making do with $15,000 or less a year when we know that the poverty level in Canada applies to any family with less than $22,000 or $23,000 a year, depending on the number of children in the family.
As I see it, Mr. Speaker, just to be sure that the Government will do something at least for men and women who live below the poverty level, it should tell these families that any person who earns less than $23,500 a year, as advocated by the Senate committee on poverty, should get a sales tax rebate from the Government. Otherwise, Mr. Speaker, it will become quite clear that this Government failed to react when the people urged it to repeal the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption which can only help those who are already well-to-do, the rich in our society.
Mr. Speaker, if we look at the Order of the Day since the Conservatives are in power-
Since taking office in 1984, we see what the Conservative Party has really intended for families in this country. The tightening and redirecting of family allowances with a review during the summer of 1986, which serves as a potential precursor of a further erosion in family allowances. The tightening and reduction of unemployment insurance benefits to those 50,000 people who were denied unemployment insurance benefits in 1986 because of a unilateral, dictatorial government action to include pension as income for the purpose of unemployment insurance calculation without even waiting for the Forget Commission Report. I am pleased to learn that the Forget Commission has recommended to the Government that pension not be included as income for those
50,000	Canadians who were cut off in 1986 as a result of the Wilson Budget and the Mulroney decisions on the unemployment insurance. I hope that the Government will follow their advice. I urge every one of those 50,000 people to write to their
November 3, 1986

Member of Parliament and tell them that they want the Government to accept the recommendation which would ensure that at the very least all those who were affected in 1986-87 and 1988 will not have their benefits cut back and reduced.
We have heard the horror stories in the House. We have heard the horror stories from individual families and from the people in my own riding who were employed at Miracle Mart, some with 15, 20 or 25 years service who have been cut loose without a penny and told to find other jobs. But they cannot collect unemployment insurance even when many of them have put their small severance pay into a nest-egg so that they could retire with some dignity.
In the time that this Government has been in office there have been severe cut-backs to job training generally, and in particular to employment programs for youth and women. A few weeks ago in the House we heard the Minister saying that the Government was introducing these new programs for women. He did not tell the people that it was this Government that withdrew programs for women as one of the first acts of its changes to the delivery system in the Canadian Jobs Strategy situation.
Social housing is another area. The impact of these cumulative sales taxes, as well as the decision by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to increase the individual guarantees anywhere from 1.5 per cent to 3 per cent on the purchase of a new home, have added several thousand dollars to the cost of a new home. When you have a situation, as we do now in the City of Toronto, where the real estate market has increased by 30 per cent in the last year, and where most average Torontonians have to come up with somewhere in the neighbourhood of $120,000 to purchase an average home, home ownership is indeed becoming a Canadian dream that will not see fruition and reality under the policies of this Government. Specifically with respect to social housing-

First, the Tory Government turned over the full responsibility for social housing to the provinces; now, it is doing the same thing concerning older workers.
The federal Government states that it wants to withdraw, to surrender the responsibility to the provinces, claiming that they know better the housing situation on their own territory. This sounds like a great idea. The only problem is that the Federal Government should sign first an agreement with all the provinces. Some provinces, like British Columbia, are not at all concerned with social housing. If we, as Members of Parliament, truly believe that there should be a national policy on social housing, we do not have the right to surrender our responsibilities to any provincial Government whatsoever.
Mr. Speaker, the same thing is now happening to older workers.

The Minister of Finance made another pronouncement. Millions of dollars are saved by eliminating the Labour Adjustment Benefits Program. In the last federal Budget the Minister said that we are doing away with the Labour Adjustment Benefits Program. It is costing too much money. Instead, we are going to replace it with a program called Program of Older Workers' Adjustment. The Minister said in his Budget that a POWA replacement program would be in place in August of 1986 to assist those hundreds of thousands of older workers who have been laid off and disenfranchised and are completely fed up with a society that even after the recession says to them, "I am sorry, you are going to have to face an unemployment rate that is double what it was before the recession". We have not seen POWA.

Mr. Speaker, have I ever had an opportunity to tell you a little about my constituency? I see you nodding your head, Mr. Speaker; I guess I have. Notwithstanding that fact, I will remind you of a few things about my constituency.
The riding of York East is situated in the geographic centre of Metropolitan Toronto. One of its characteristics is the fact that there are more jobs per thousand residents in my constituency than anywhere else in the whole of Metropolitan Toronto, with the exception of the downtown financial core. It is a very industrialized riding.
Some of the businesses and industries in my riding are very large ones, such as IBM. Others-in fact many hundreds of them-are quite small with only a few employees or workers. Many of the workers in the small plants and in the larger ones are worried at the moment. They are worried about the trade negotiations which we are undertaking with the United States. They are worried about what the press likes to call "free trade". They are also worried because they do not know what might happen to their jobs as a result of these trade negotiations.
A few days ago they heard from the Economic Council of Canada. Unfortunately, they do not feel much better as a result of those comments. The Economic Council of Canada said that it was quite possible that some 370,000 new jobs could be created by 1995 as a result of a new trade agreement with the United States. However, the Council also said that all Canadians must be sensitive to the prospect that some citizens will lose their businesses or their jobs as a result of more competition from lower cost United States-made goods entering Canada.
That is a sobering thought, especially if one thought that one's job or business might be affected by the trade negotiations. What would you do, Mr. Speaker, if you lost your job as a result? I know that you are a young man and that you could be retrained. Perhaps that is what you are thinking, that you would go through a retraining program. However, many of my constituents do not see themselves in your age category. They think of themselves as older workers, and they believe it would be impossible for them to retrain. Perhaps they are looking to some special government programs to help them, perhaps special retraining programs. They have not heard anything from the Government as yet about what sort of special retraining programs might be available. They also wonder if there might be some financial assistance for them as a result of what could happen through the trade negotiations. Again they have not heard anything specific from the Government about what those programs might be.
However, they have heard some people say: "Businesses go bankrupt every day. People lose their jobs every day. How can we tell who are the people losing their jobs as a result of trade negotiations and who are the people losing their jobs through
inefficiency, lack of good management, or whatever?". These same people say that there is not much point in trying to assist people financially or through retraining programs because they cannot tell whether they are losing their jobs for other reasons or through the trade negotiations. My constituents have heard those comments and are disturbed by them.
They have also heard comments from other people who ask why we should assist businesses which go bankrupt or people who lose their jobs through the trade negotiations, because it will only increase the cost for the winners in the process and they will not be able to afford to compete with the Americans after the negotiations. They are worried by those comments as well.
How are we, Mr. Speaker, you and I, going to reassure our constituents that these trade negotiations are going to be of benefit to them? How are we going to tell them that everything is going to be okay? I think the Government can start by telling you and me and all of our constituents what it calculates both the job gains and job losses to be as a result of these trade negotiations. It can also tell us which industries it believes as a result of its studies are going to be the winning industries and which are going to be the losing industries. Most of all, I think it should be telling us how it is going to cushion the blow. Are we going to have retraining programs? If so, for whom and what kind, and how do people qualify? Are we going to have financial assistance? If so, what is it going to be? Those are the questions that you, I and our constituents are asking, and I know that tonight you and 1 are waiting with bated breath to hear the answers from the Government.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a pity that you cannot give the answer because I am sure in your previous position as a very important part of the Edmonton Eskimo machine you must have had a lot to do with international trade. Probably. Anyway, the answer I have to give here is the following.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext:
The section of the Economic Council of Canada annual review dealing with Canada's trade experience and opportunities discussed the impact of several Canada-U.S. trade scenarios on GNP and employment, based on computer simulations. These simulations made various assumptions, the most favourable of which, such as the removal of trade barriers plus productivity gains, led to an assumed increase in employment of 376,000 by 1995. Other assumptions, such as gradual removal of trade barriers plus productivity gains, removal of trade barriers with no productivity gain, and protectionism with retaliation, all led to different results ranging from an increase in employment by 1995 of 321,000, to a net loss of jobs totalling 528,000.
All such studies based on computer simulations or econometric models make assumptions about how such key elements
November 3, 1986

as productivity, exchange rates, investment and prices respond to the elimination of tariff and non-tariff barriers. Some recent studies include projections done by the University of Maryland, Informetric, and the University of Toronto, as well as those done by the Economic Council of Canada. While estimates of the impact of freer trade on employment vary owing to variations in inputs, the common thread running through all the studies done so far is that freer trade would produce an over-all net national employment gain of between 1 per cent and 3 per cent of the current employment level. With a current employment level of about 11.5 million, that translates into between 115,000 and 345,00 additional jobs.
There, Sir, is your answer.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-PAY-OUTS IN ATLANTIC CANADA. (B) REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE

speechtext:
Mir. Rod Murphy (Churchill): Mr. Speaker, I cannot help but add to the comments between the Conservative Member who asked the previous question and the Conservative Member who responded on behalf of the Government. He said that you, as a former member of the Edmonton Eskimos, would know how to deal with the problems that Canadians face in keeping jobs in Canada with regard to free trade negotiations. It reminded me, with the greatest respect, that we did guarantee there would be Canadian jobs for people playing for Canadian teams. That was kind of a Canadian content measure. I am sure that you, Mr. Speaker, would have kept your job even without that particular piece of legislation, but others who played for the Canadian Football League did need that sort of protection.
I rise to speak in regard to a question I asked on October 15 of this year. It resulted from the leaking of certain information regarding the Forget Commission. There have been indications that the report of the Forget Commission will result in a drastic change in the way with which unemployment insurance is dealt. This concerns me and my Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), so much so that we both asked questions that day in the House of Commons.
We pointed out that Atlantic Canada receives approximately $620 million from the Unemployment Insurance Program. We wanted a guarantee from the Government that that amount of money would continue to go to Atlantic Canada through similar programs if not through the Unemployment Insurance Program. We also spoke at that time about the need to recognize the very fragile economy in Atlantic Canada. The fishery, forestry and mining industries, as well as the small business and other sectors, have relied on part-time and seasonal work for a very long time, and that is not likely to change overnight. We said that regardless of what the federal Government does as a result of the Forget Commission, it must take that into account.
It is not only me and the Leader of the New Democratic Party who are concerned about the Forget Commission. I
Adjournment Debate
could quote people from across the land, but one of the most interesting quotes is from the Conservative Minister of Social Services in Nova Scotia, Edmund Morris, who said that this could "wreak havoc on the economy of Nova Scotia".
This is a very serious matter. The fishery and forestry industries have relied on seasonal work for a very long time. The economy of that part of Canada is not changing quickly. The people in that area will continue to rely on unemployment insurance. We are not happy about that or proud of it. However, we are concerned that whatever the Government does as a result of the Forget Commission take into account the economy and job situation which exists in Atlantic Canada. We hope that as a result of the work of the Forget Commission the Government will do all it can to enhance, rather than destroy, that which presently exists in Atlantic Canada.
I raise this issue again at this time because, in response to my questions and those of the Hon. Member for Oshawa, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) would not give us those assurances. The Minister was right to say that he cannot respond completely to the report of the Forget Commission which has not yet come down. However, he could have taken the opportunity to say, in response to our questions, that there will be certain protections for Atlantic Canada, to guarantee that $620 million will still go to that region and to guarantee that there will be some new job creation programs for that region. He did not do that, Mr. Speaker, and that is one of the reasons I raise this issue at this time.
In addition, I believe the people of Atlantic Canada are still very nervous as a result of the scant mention they received in the Throne Speech. The leaks from the Forget Commission indicated that the Government must get up in the House and explain what it is going to do. I am afraid that the Government's response will be that we cannot allow the unemployment insurance program to continue as it is year after year. I am afraid that the Government will admit that there are problems in Atlantic Canada but will say that it will not deal with the problems of the mine workers, small business and the others involved in various industries in Atlantic Canada. Instead, the Government will talk about the need to reform unemployment insurance.
It is not good enough to talk about the need to reform unemployment insurance. The people of Atlantic Canada are demanding from the Government a clear indication of where it is going. Unemployment has not been reduced in Atlantic Canada in the two years during which the Government has been in power. It is one of the regions that has not benefited from the general improvement in the economy. Frankly, they are very nervous about the Government's intentions and are very concerned that there has been no set direction with regard to what is happening in Atlantic Canada.
Adjournment Debate
It is fine for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to say in the Throne Speech that Atlantic Canada will be considered and there will be a new agency set up to see what can be done for Atlantic Canada. The truth is, however, that the Government has been in power for two years and if it is going to do anything for Atlantic Canada it must do so soon, not in a few months prior to an election. If the Government has a plan of action for Atlantic Canada, Quebec and other parts of the country, this is the year for it to act. We want to hear what it will do.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-PAY-OUTS IN ATLANTIC CANADA. (B) REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to some of the comments by the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy), in conjunction with the answer that was already supplied to him by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard).

The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made it very clear, in referring to the comments of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his May 23, 1985 Budget Speech, that the Government has no intention of reducing its support to the unemployed anywhere in Canada. It will not do that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comments this evening are based not only on the most recent
November 3, 1986
question but a series of questions that I asked in the House following the collapse of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Government's unprecedented action in paying out $1 billion to uninsured depositors whose names are being kept secret.
By now we are all too well aware of the circumstances of the bank's failure less than six months after the Government bailed it out and guaranteed its viability. Since then I have asked over 50 questions in the House. I have participated in other adjournment debates and in debate on the Bills brought before the House to deal with the bank bail-out and later, the bail-out of uninsured depositors.
The Government's record of providing answers to my questions and those put by my colleagues has been consistently poor. We were told that all our questions would be answered by a special inquiry. First we were promised a parliamentary inquiry. Then the Government appointed the Estey Commission and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said in the House on October 2 of last year, and it is found in Hansard at page 7250:
-the Government appointed Mr. Justice Estey with the broadest possible terms of reference so that the full truth can come out, including the conduct of everyone involved and the policies that went into the matter. Mr. Justice Estey will put the spotlight on those people who are responsible.
We have the Estey Report now and, indeed, it is for the most part a very thorough and illuminating document. It confirms much of what we have said in the House about the bail-out being undertaken in an atmosphere of panic and haste without proper information or adequate follow-up.
The report does not answer all of our questions, but the position of the Government appears to be that now the report is public, the case is closed. This is not so. I agree with Mr. Justice Estey when he says in his report at page 21:
It may be that other forums-having different objectives will reach different conclusions with respect to duties and obligations of the participants in these events.
I am not prepared to close the book on the bank failures and the bail-out of uninsured depositors because the principle of ministerial accountability is at the heart of our parliamentary system. That principle is not being observed.
The Government has made much of the fact that the Estey Report does not put blame on Ministers for events prior to the CCB bail-out. However, the report condemns in no uncertain terms the way in which the decision to bail out the bank was reached. It condemns the bail-out package itself and the almost total lack of follow-up action from the Government. The report says about the bail-out, at page 125:
The concept adopted was-at best half baked.
And at page 127:
-this bail-out was ill-starred from the outset and had no chance of success.
And at page 174:

November 3, 1986

The bail-out program seems to have been conducted more like the launching of a toboggan. Once it was placed on the slope, its course, speed and destination were left to gravity and the toboggan. There was no steering mechanism and no machinery for change of direction or increased financial support or indeed any other adjustment, whatever risk may loom up.
And on page 173:
-the Minister of State appears to have made no effort to press for an early and organized hands-on examination of the loan assets of the bank.
That was after the bail-out was decided upon. And at page 175 it says:
The combination of the lack of information at the time the rescue program was adopted and announced, and the tenor of that announcement and subsequent statements by the Ministers-boxed the Government into a position where the only defensible alternative was universal compensation of creditors of the bank.
Under a system of ministerial accountability, someone has to be in charge. Our traditional notion of ministerial accountability says that Ministers of the Crown are responsible and that ignorance of an issue, or being poorly served by officials, does not absolve a Minister from responsibility for decisions he or she has taken. This is fundamental to our system of Government and it is not acceptable for the Government to refuse to take responsibility for its actions which are costing the taxpayers close to $2 billion.
As I mentioned earlier, I and my colleagues still have questions to ask. 1 would like to have answers to those questions and some indication that the principle of ministerial accountability means something to this Government.

In her statement, the Hon. Member lost sight of the basic objective of our tax reform, which is to make each component of the taxation system, that is personal income tax, corporate income tax and the sales tax, more equitable, simpler and more efficient.
